guideTitle: The Best Digital Notebooks Under $100: Reusable Paper and Bluetooth Writing Pads
metaTitle: Best Digital Notebooks Under $100: Rocketbook, XPPen and Huion (2026)
metaDescription: Under $100 there are no E Ink tablets, but reusable Rocketbook notebooks and Bluetooth writing pads can still digitize handwriting. We compare how each captures and exports notes.
introParagraphs: Set expectations first: there is no E Ink writing tablet like a reMarkable under $100. What this budget buys is either a reusable Rocketbook notebook, where you write on special paper, scan pages with a phone app and wipe them clean, or a Bluetooth writing pad from XPPen or Huion that records handwriting and syncs it to your phone.

The choice comes down to how notes should reach your phone. Rocketbooks cost $15 to $27 at the time of writing and need a scan step; the XPPen and Huion pads cost more and capture notes as you write. Very cheap LCD "writing tablets" that cannot save anything are not included.
Our comparison is based on published specifications, included accessories and price position, not hands-on testing.

b0dp3jf67q-under100dn.summary: A letter-size reusable Rocketbook that you scan with an app and wipe clean.
b0dp3jf67q-under100dn.description:
The letter-size Rocketbook Core is the sensible default: full 8.5 x 11-inch pages you write on, scan with the Rocketbook app and wipe with a damp cloth, for about $27 at the time of writing.

The full page leaves plenty of room for meeting notes or sketches, and notes can be sent from the app to cloud services.

It needs a compatible erasable pen, and notes only become digital when you scan them.
specs: Reusable pages, erase with damp cloth
b0dp3jf67q-under100dn.bestFor: Most note-takers who want handwritten notes on their phone for little money.
b0dp3jf67q-under100dn.skipIf: You want notes to sync as you write; the XPPen Note Plus does that.

b0dp3hly4j-under100dn.summary: The same Rocketbook Core system in a 6 x 8.8-inch executive size.
b0dp3hly4j-under100dn.description:
The executive-size Rocketbook Core works exactly like the letter-size version in a smaller 6 x 8.8-inch format that is easier to carry, and it costs slightly less at the time of writing.

The smaller page means more frequent scanning and erasing if you write a lot.

It has fewer buyer reviews than the letter-size and mini Rocketbooks.
b0dp3hly4j-under100dn.bestFor: People who carry a notebook between meetings or classes.
b0dp3hly4j-under100dn.skipIf: You need room to spread out; the letter-size Core is larger for about a dollar more.

b07czf628c-under100dn.summary: A mini spiral Rocketbook for quick notes, for about $15.
b07czf628c-under100dn.description:
The Rocketbook Mini is the cheapest way to try the system: a small spiral notebook for quick notes and lists, for about $15 at the time of writing. It is widely reviewed.

It uses the same scan-and-erase routine as the larger Rocketbooks.

The small page fills quickly, so it suits lists and reminders better than long notes.
b07czf628c-under100dn.bestFor: Trying reusable notebooks, or keeping a pocket notebook for lists.
b07czf628c-under100dn.skipIf: You take long notes; a Core notebook gives more space.

b0gcdrfjqg-under100dn.summary: A writing pad with pen that syncs handwriting to your phone over Bluetooth.
b0gcdrfjqg-under100dn.description:
The XPPen Note Plus is the pick if the scanning step is what puts you off a Rocketbook: it is a writing pad with a pen that syncs your handwriting to your phone over Bluetooth, for about $70 at the time of writing.

It is widely reviewed for its category. It is not an E Ink tablet, and the listing does not detail export formats or handwriting-to-text conversion, so check XPPen's app features for what you need.

It costs more than any Rocketbook, and the pen or pad may need charging; check the listing for power details.
specs: Type: Bluetooth writing pad with pen
cons: App features and export formats not detailed in the listing
b0gcdrfjqg-under100dn.bestFor: People who want notes on their phone as they write without paying for an E Ink tablet.
b0gcdrfjqg-under100dn.skipIf: You are happy to scan pages; a Rocketbook costs far less.

b0bg2t9sgv-under100dn.summary: A Huion notebook-and-drawing tablet with a battery-free pen.
b0bg2t9sgv-under100dn.description:
The Huion Note is the choice if you also want to draw: a 2-in-1 digital notebook and drawing tablet with a battery-free pen, so the pen never needs charging.

It costs about $88 at the time of writing, the most here, and buyer feedback is slightly less positive than for the XPPen.

As with the XPPen, check Huion's app and export options against how you plan to use your notes.
cons: Slightly weaker buyer feedback than the XPPen
b0bg2t9sgv-under100dn.bestFor: Students or creatives who want note capture and a drawing tablet in one.
b0bg2t9sgv-under100dn.skipIf: You only take notes; the XPPen costs less.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Rocketbooks need a phone scan after writing; the XPPen and Huion pads capture notes as you write.
Rocketbooks here come in letter (8.5 x 11 inches), executive (6 x 8.8 inches) and mini sizes.
Check where notes can go (cloud services, PDF, note apps) and whether handwriting-to-text is included or costs extra.
Rocketbooks need a compatible erasable pen. The Huion's pen is battery-free; check the XPPen listing for charging details.

faq.q: Can I get an E Ink smart notebook under $100?
faq.a: Not new, at the time of writing. Under $100 the realistic choices are reusable paper notebooks and Bluetooth writing pads.

faq.q: What's the closest thing to a digital notebook under $100?
faq.a: The XPPen Note Plus, which syncs handwriting to your phone over Bluetooth instead of requiring a scan.

faq.q: What's the cheapest option that still captures notes?
faq.a: The Rocketbook Mini, at about $15 at the time of writing.
Rocketbooks require you to scan each page with the app before erasing. The XPPen and Huion pads sync to your phone as you write.

faq.q: Are there cheap writing tablets that can't save notes?
faq.a: Yes. Basic LCD writing pads often cannot save or export anything. None are included here.

bottomLine: For most people, a Rocketbook is enough: the letter-size Core for general notes, the executive size for carrying, or the Mini to try the system for about $15.
If scanning each page is the obstacle, the XPPen Note Plus syncs as you write for about $70, and the Huion Note adds drawing-tablet use with a battery-free pen at the top of the budget.
